summary_html: A **state agency fails** to meet federal child-welfare performance standards, triggering **funding penalties** or corrective action under the CFSR or Single Audit Act.
authority_html:
- **Child & Family Services Reviews (45 CFR Part 1355)** — performance oversight and penalties  
- **Single Audit Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 7501–7507)** — audit of federally funded programs  
- **Inspector General Act (5 U.S.C. App.)** — oversight authority for HHS/OIG

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's 'reasonable efforts' requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no right enforceable by foster children either directly or through 42 U.S.C. § 1983.
key_cases.relevance: Suter is the controlling authority on what happens when a state fails federal child welfare standards: the remedy lies with the federal funding agency, not with private plaintiffs.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

key_cases.case_name: Sam M. ex rel. Elliott v. Carcieri
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: The district court abused its discretion in refusing to let the proposed next friends represent children in DCYF custody and in dismissing their systemic class action; the complaint was reinstated and the next friends appointed.
key_cases.relevance: Systemic failure claims against DCYF proceed as next-friend class actions because the federal plan requirements are not individually enforceable.
key_cases.quote: We remand the case with directions to reinstate the complaint and allow Ms. Melvin, Ms. Collins, and Dr. Elliott to proceed as the children's Next Friends.

key_cases.case_name: Danny B. ex rel. Elliott v. Raimondo
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: In the Rhode Island foster care class action, the district court abused its discretion by completely barring the plaintiff foster children from communicating with their own lawyers before trial, and the resulting prejudice required reversal.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading recent First Circuit decision on litigating Rhode Island's child welfare system-wide performance.
key_cases.quote: We hold, therefore, that the court below abused its discretion when it completely denied the plaintiffs access to their lawyers prior to trial.

key_cases.case_name: Connor B. Ex Rel. Vigurs v. Patrick
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: Judgment on the record for the state child welfare defendants was affirmed because the foster children's class did not prove a substantial departure from accepted professional judgment under Youngberg, and class-wide liability is a precursor to any systemic injunctive relief.
key_cases.relevance: This is the First Circuit's most recent merits treatment of a claim that a state child welfare system fails federal and constitutional standards, and it explains why such claims rarely succeed even when performance data are poor.
key_cases.quote: Not only has class-wide liability not been shown, itself a needed precursor to any relief, but plaintiffs have also not met the requirements for injunctive relief.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Reversing, the Court held that a federal spending statute creates a section 1983-enforceable right only when it unambiguously confers one in individually focused, rights-creating terms, and FERPA's nondisclosure provisions, which speak to the Secretary of Education, do not.
key_cases.relevance: Gonzaga supplies the test that now decides whether a Rhode Island failure to meet a federal child welfare standard is privately actionable at all, replacing the looser 'zone of interest' reading some courts drew from Blessing.
key_cases.quote: We now reject the notion that our cases permit anything short of an unambiguously conferred right to support a cause of action brought under §1983.

key_cases.case_name: Health and Hospital Corporation of Marion Cty. v. Talevski
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Spending Clause statutes can create rights enforceable under section 1983; the Federal Nursing Home Reform Act's unnecessary-restraint and predischarge-notice provisions unambiguously confer individual rights, and the Act's own enforcement scheme does not foreclose a section 1983 suit, so the judgment for the resident was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: Talevski is the controlling modern statement of when a state's failure to meet a federal child welfare standard can be remedied by a private suit rather than only by federal funding action.
key_cases.quote: our precedent sets a demanding bar: Statutory provisions must unambiguously confer individual federal rights.
